title: Tate brothers officially indicted with trafficking and sex crimes in Romania
description: The brothers - former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship - have been under criminal investigation in Romania since December 2022. They ha
body: The brothers - former kickboxers with dual US and British citizenship - have been under criminal investigation in Romania since December 2022. They have been mainly based there since 2017, drawing a large social media audience - many of them young men - through misogynistic messages and images of a luxury lifestyle.Romanian prosecutors described a case as centring on a vulnerable female who was 15 at the time of the alleged offence, in information released on Friday.She is alleged to have been recruited by Andrew and housed in a building in Luton, Bedfordshire, so he could sexually exploit her. Tristan is alleged to have been an accessory, prosecutors say, using physical aggression to coerce the victim.DIICOT investigators allege Andrew controlled her through surveillance and physical aggression, and coerced her to perform sex acts on video chats for his financial gain.Andrew is also accused of moving her to Romania to carry on exploiting her in two of his homes.He is separately charged with having sex with a minor, who was 15, in Romania.Prosecutors have also requested four of the brothers' luxury cars worth £710,000 be confiscated. They believe money was laundered through their purchase.The two brothers were previously indicted in Romania on trafficking charges, but in 2024 an appeals court in Bucharest sent the case back to prosecutors after deeming some evidence inadmissible.It is not yet clear if DIICOT will seek their extradition from the US and the indictment has to be examined by a judge before any trial can begin. The Tates have denied all the allegations and say their online personas are not their real personalities.Their lawyer in Romania, Eugen Constantin Vidineac, said: "Today's decision by DIICOT does not determine guilt and it should not be presented as though it does. It represents the prosecution's latest attempt to bring this case before a court following the failure of its previous indictment to proceed to trial."The history of these proceedings matters. The previous indictment was subjected to judicial scrutiny and the court identified significant irregularities which prevented the case from moving forward to trial."DIICOT has now chosen to file a new indictment. We will examine every aspect of it with the same level of scrutiny and we will challenge any evidential, procedural or legal deficiencies through the appropriate judicial process."Our clients continue to reject the allegations against them. They have the right to the presumption of innocence, the right to properly examine the evidence relied upon against them and the right to mount an effective defence."Correction 5 September: A previous version of this article incorrectly stated that the Tate brothers were charged with further offences. The article has been updated to make clear they have been officially indicted with offences of which they had already been accused. It has also been updated to reflect that Andrew, not Tristan, was alleged to have recruited the 15-year-old.

schema.headline: Tate brothers officially indicted with trafficking and sex crimes in Romania

title: Virgin's Richard Branson: Flight price rises due to 'foolish leaders' starting wars
description: Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson has blamed flight price rises on "foolish leaders" starting wars, in a thinly veiled reference to the US-Isra
body: Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson has blamed flight price rises on "foolish leaders" starting wars, in a thinly veiled reference to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.Middle East tensions have choked the production and transportation of millions of barrels of oil, causing a surge in the price of car and jet fuels, which are made from oil.In May, Virgin Atlantic added a fuel surcharge to ticket prices in response.US President Donald Trump has repeatedly defended the conflict as necessary for peace and security long-term.However, Sir Richard said there was "no need" for the war. "The Iran conflict was completely unnecessary. There was a nuclear agreement between Iran and the rest of the world that had been negotiated by President Obama and a lot of European people."It was working, so there was no need to rip it up... And this war has just resulted in much higher oil prices all over the world. And inflation has been one of the consequences."The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.The European benchmark jet fuel price had been hovering around $800 (£590) a tonne but spiked following the outbreak of the Iran war, reaching a peak of over $1,800 in April. It has since dropped to around $1,450. Virgin Atlantic's chief executive, Corneel Koster, told the BBC that for "this level of fuel price" fuel surcharges were "absolutely required", adding that it's "hard to be optimistic at this moment about the situation in the Middle East".The surcharge Virgin introduced added £50 to an economy class fare, £180 to premium and £360 to business class.

schema.headline: Virgin's Richard Branson: Flight price rises due to 'foolish leaders' starting wars

title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
description: A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before collidin
body: A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news."No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra £2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra £20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.It also ranks highest for burglary, sexual offences, violence with injury, and criminal damage and arson.Fuller said Cleveland Police had also experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force."It absolutely needs to change," she said. Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."Recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues."We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fuelling organised crime."When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said. "They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."The five who died in the Volkswagen on 22 August were aged between 17 and 23. Four of them had previous convictions, including for assaulting police officers and theft, Cleveland Police previously said.Since the crash, the force has responded to at least two incidents it believes are in retaliation for the crash.It has also had to grapple with a house fire in Middlesbrough that killed a woman and her niece, and left several others injured, which police could not rule out was linked to organised crime.A 23-year-old man has been charged with murder in relation to the deaths of Natalie McDonald, 34, and Valentina Foster, seven.Fuller also paid tribute to the two officers who died in the A66 crash - PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough."My heart goes out to their families - it really does," she said. "My grief can't compare to theirs, nor to the officers and staff who've worked closely with Matty and Tom for a long time."The Home Office said it was grateful to Cleveland Police for delivering a robust response in difficult circumstances. A spokesperson said: "We have been in regular contact with Cleveland Police and local leaders, ensuring they have the support they need and engaging on their financial concerns."This additional £2m targeted funding will help Cleveland Police tackle serious crime. Beyond this, the force will receive up to £197.8m in funding in the 2026/2027 financial year - a 3.7% uplift in cash."We have also committed to a wider review of the police funding formula to ensure that force funding is fair and responsive to local needs."

schema.headline: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding

title: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong
description: The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate
body: The now widely used Mercator map was created in 1569 by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator.Its main purpose was to help European sailors navigate the oceans, as cartography Professor James Cheshire at University London College explained."He wanted a straight line to be drawn on a map to look like a straight line in reality if you followed a compass bearing," he told the BBC. "That was what it was intended to do, and that's what it does brilliantly well."To keep those angles correct on a flat map, Mercator had to stretch the grid lines wider as they moved away from the equator toward the poles.His map accommodates for the curvature of the Earth by making countries near the equator seem much smaller than they are, with countries nearer the poles appearing stretched.The distortion is a result of it being impossible to accurately represent the surface of a globe on a two-dimensional chart.More than 450 years on, Mercator's creation is still the basis for many of the maps we see in classrooms, on TV and online, including Google Maps.But critics of the Mercator map say there is a psychological effect to viewing some places as smaller than they actually are and others as larger, as we instinctively view bigger things as more important.For Kenyan geographer Kioko Muendo, this has implicitly downplayed Africa's vast resources, population and investment opportunities."Maps are more than just guides for travellers - they shape how regions are perceived politically and economically," he told the BBC.

schema.headline: What different world maps get right - and what they get wrong

title: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder
description: That position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course,
body: That position has traditionally been one of neutrality - albeit while recognising Britain's rule over the territory. "Neutral" is relative, of course, given that President Reagan provided material support to Margaret Thatcher during the Falklands War in 1982  – an act which reinforced the long-standing alliance between London and Washington in times of conflict.For Trump, however, that mutual support – the "Special Relationship" – was eroded by Sir Keir Starmer when the UK Government chose not to join the US war on Iran."You weren't there to help me", the president retorted in an interview with GB News this week. The Falklands were "a long way away", he said. The Falkland Islanders – who voted almost unanimously to remain a British overseas territory in 2013 – would point out that distance from London to the Falklands is fractionally shorter than the distance between Washington DC and the US territory of Guam, in the western Pacific.Still, Trump's words have undoubtedly galvanised Milei. As have the opinion polls. He urgently needs a boost ahead of a presidential election next year in which one of his challengers, his estranged vice-president, Victoria Villarruel, has presented herself as a tougher defender of national sovereignty and attacked Milei's diplomatic approach on the Falklands as failing.Domestic politics can rarely be ruled out of the equation when the Falklands issue flares back up. However, Buenos Aires argues that the matter has become urgent: "A clear and urgent danger", as Milei put it.With two energy companies – the Israeli-owned Navitas Petroleum and Rockhopper Exploration from the UK – due to undertake work on the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, the issue has new impetus. Argentina "cannot allow" the companies to "appropriate the oil reserves under our sea", he said. "We will not stand by with our arms folded," he added.On Saturday morning Milei's office said on X that it was launching sanctions proceedings against 45 people and companies. The announcement did not identify those targeted and it is not yet clear what impact they will have.In his speech, Javier Milei painted Argentina as a reliable and "trustworthy partner" to Washington and he enjoys Trump's support, both ideologically and personally. The two men are close allies in a vision of the Western Hemisphere which Trump calls the "Don-roe Doctrine", a play on words on the 19th Century 'Monroe Doctrine' which exerted American domination over the continent. In essence, the two presidents want to see only like-minded leaders in power in the Americas.Within such a new partnership and a reordering of the spheres of influence, it's more than conceivable that Trump favours the Argentine leader over the British Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, even if the issues at play transcend personality and party politics.Perhaps the key question for the coming months, then, is whether the strength of the so-called "Don-roe Doctrine" outweighs the lasting history of the "Special Relationship".

schema.headline: Trump's response is key as Argentina's Falklands demands get louder

title: Sibling rivalry: When parents play financial favourites
description: 'My parents won't lend me £10k but helped my brother': When families play financial favouritesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, One US study su
body: 'My parents won't lend me £10k but helped my brother': When families play financial favouritesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, One US study suggests around 15% of siblings have had conflicts over moneyByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsDo your parents have a favourite child and give them more money, gifts or help?Financial favouritism can cause jealousy and resentment long into adulthood and, in some cases, even spark legal disputes after a parent dies. But experts say there are strategies that can help you avoid it.John says his parents, who have always supported his younger brother, recently refused to lend him £10,000 towards a house deposit after he broke up with his partner.This was despite the money being "well within their financial grasp", he says.His parents had previously given his brother a deposit to buy a home and subsidised his living expenses.John, 47, whose real name we have changed, says he was viewed as the more academic one growing up and expected to stand on his "own two feet" financially, while his brother, 42, struggled to make his way in the world and was "coddled".He says the favouritism has made him believe "the needs of others take precedence over my own", leaving him feeling "isolated" and affecting friendships and romantic relationships.'Powerful emotional meaning'Forums like Mumsnet and Reddit, external are full of posts complaining about siblings being shown preferential treatment regarding money. Common gripes include the amount of financial support adult children have received, external from their parents during their lifetime, the way inheritance is divided, external, and whether a sibling has supported their parents more than others, external.Dr Fenia Christodoulidi, from counselling service Relate, says that disagreements about money between siblings are rarely just about the money itself.  "Financial support from parents often carries a powerful emotional meaning and some siblings tend to interpret differences in support as signs of favouritism, unequal love or a lack of recognition." She adds that even when parents have "practical reasons" for treating their children differently, failing to communicate these clearly can "leave room for misunderstanding and resentment".Those reasons might include an adult child needing more support because they earn significantly less, have an illness, or have to pay more to get on the housing ladder due to rising prices, external.'It's never been a problem'Image caption, Ellis, 26, says there is no financial favourite in her familyEllis, who works in finance in London, tells the BBC that she and her siblings have had "different levels of support at different times" from their parents and it's never been a problem.Image caption, Tasha says her siblings have had disagreementsBut her colleague Tasha, the youngest of seven, says her siblings have fallen out over perceived favouritism, even though she thinks her parents treat them all the same."I just think people sometimes get a bit uncertain or jealous and that's quite normal," says the 33-year-old. "Sometimes people stop talking for a bit or go to process what they are feeling, and they come back together and they just hash it out."'Open conversations help'Having "open conversations about expectations and the reasons behind decisions" can help reduce feelings of resentment about money, Christodoulidi says.But for some, it's not that easy. "Talking about money is verboten in my family - be it salaries or savings or financial assistance," says John. "Any time I've tried to air my feelings my parents just become evasive so now I don't bother."John says he is now planning his financial future on the basis he won't have any inheritance - although he expects to be asked to step in if his parents get ill or lose capacity.He says he has a "great relationship with his brother" but feels resentment towards his parents for creating the "imbalance" between them.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Open conversations can help reduce feelings of resentmentClaire Webb, a solicitor and mediator at Family Solutions Now, regularly helps siblings who have disputes over inheritance and other money matters."One sibling might argue the other was given more money earlier on in life, say, to buy a house, and that the parents said this would be reflected in the will. "Then the will says, 'everything should be shared equally'. So you have all of that historic feeling of unfairness being dredged up."To avoid conflict, she says parents need to be clear with their children about what they want while they are still alive. 'A deep-down family bond'Siblings who do fall out should consider mediation before taking legal action, she adds. This is when a trained professional helps them remedy their problems.The good news is, siblings who take the legal route more often than not reach an amicable solution. "Most of the time there is a deep-down family bond - and if you can crack what started the problem they often find a way through."Tips for resolving money quarrels between siblings1. Recognise what's behind the row: It may be about feeling valued or treated fairly, rather than the money itself2. Avoid making assumptions about a sibling's financial situation or the reasons behind parental decisions3. Encourage open, respectful conversations where everyone has the opportunity to explain how they feel4. Parents should communicate their intentions as clearly as possible, particularly if they are supporting children differently for practical reasons5. Consider family counselling if conversations repeatedly become stuck or emotionally charged6. Consider mediation before taking legal action in inheritance disputes.  7. Choose powers of attorney carefully: Parents usually appoint their children to oversee their care and finances if they get ill or lose mental capacity. But if there's a risk they'll fall out, they can appoint someone else including a solicitor. Sources: Relate, Family Now Solutions

schema.headline: Sibling rivalry: When parents play financial favourites

title: Michael Owen doesn't tell his children he loves them - how big a deal is that?
description: Dad Aaron Dale, host of the Raisingboys2men podcast and author of a book on parenting, agrees."It's not words or actions - they shouldn't compete agai
body: Dad Aaron Dale, host of the Raisingboys2men podcast and author of a book on parenting, agrees."It's not words or actions - they shouldn't compete against each other, they should complement each other."Words are to speak the message and actions are the evidence."Dale pointed to how his own father would often tell him "I love you" after letting him down, diminishing the meaning of the words. However, some parents believe it is absolutely crucial their child hears that they are loved. One father of a seven-year-old daughter, told us he was surprised by Owen's comments, describing them as "awful". "You should always tell your children you love them no matter what, when they're bad, when they're good," he said. And reacting online to the clip of Owen, another parent wrote: "Parents and potential parents do not listen to this man. Tell your kids you love them everyday, even when it annoys them."To the outside observer, Owen's love for his children is not in doubt.The trailer for his new show, Meet the Owens, shows glimpses of what appears to be a happy home life with his wife and children. And in 2024, the former England striker spoke movingly about his son James's sight loss, saying: "If I could give him my eyes... I would."Pushed by podcast host Laing to explain why he doesn't let the 'I love yous' flow freely, Owen told Laing that "I would love to be a little bit soft"."I'm definitely getting softer," he said, "but still not soft enough to say anything like that."Using the word "soft" to describe telling your children you love them reflects long-standing attitudes many fathers have towards parenting, both Dale and Dr Britto suggest. They say it's a result of different contexts, such as culture, class, gender and a generational divide"I think that's the dangerous part there," Dale says, "the belief of what men should and what men shouldn't do."Many fathers believe their role is simply to "provide", but they can do so much more, he says. "Men are much more than just providers... what about our emotional capacity and willingness to have conversations and be there as fathers? And maybe we can't provide, but you know what? Our presence is at full capacity." He adds that he thinks people's style of parenting "always stems from somewhere", including whether they were often told they were loved as a child.Gender expectations and masculinity are not the only element at play, Dr Britto says."In some cultures they don't even use those words [I love you] at all," she says. "They may ask things like 'Have you eaten?' as a sign of love rather than actually saying 'I love you'."She adds: "As an African myself, in Nigerian culture parents don't always say 'I love you'... but I still felt loved."Parents also suggest that different generations may approach showing love for their children in different ways. Reacting on social media, one says Owen is right to suggest actions speak louder than words: "My dad never said the words, but it was also never in doubt."Another writes: "What's the big deal? My dad - and I'm sure most dads of our generation - didn't. He did something far, far better than emotional words he 'showed us' by his actions."While Owen's comments may have triggered strong feelings, it is clear there are countless ways parents communicate love to their children.Above all, says Dr Britto, it's about making sure children feel a sense of belonging. "Do they feel loved?" she says. "Do they feel wanted? "Do they feel that they matter, rather than simply hearing the words?"

schema.headline: Michael Owen doesn't tell his children he loves them - how big a deal is that?

title: A66 crash: Distrust and fear hang over Middlesbrough
description: It is just after 8pm in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, and the light is fading.Two teenagers in balaclavas tear across a park on a muddy red quad bik
body: It is just after 8pm in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, and the light is fading.Two teenagers in balaclavas tear across a park on a muddy red quad bike, pulling wheelies as they pass a man walking his dog.Younger boys, some not yet in their teens, gather excitedly around the bike.We're here because Grangetown and neighbouring South Bank now find themselves at the centre of a large police operation, with fears organised crime is out of control after the deaths of two police officers and five young men in a car crash on the A66.Suddenly one of our team is hit by a pellet, which appears to have been fired from the group. It stings but he's OK.Then the quad riders pull over for a chat, engine running.I ask the riders if it is normal to be driving around the park on a quad bike."Yeah, this isn't any special day," the passenger says. "You're born and bred and brought up with it. What do you expect? You don't know anything different."Since the crash, more than 20 people have been arrested in Middlesbrough and the surrounding area as part of a wider operation into what police have called "serious and organised crime".Sources say there are two feuding gangs at the centre of a spike in violence.Is this area out of control, I ask the quad bike riders. "No. Definitely not."Then they reveal something we repeatedly heard from young people here. They do not trust the police."They're saying there are gangs, but there are no gangs," the driver says. "It's not London, mate. Do you know what I mean?"Like many young people here, they blame the police for the deaths on the A66. The circumstances remain under independent investigation.What we do know is that on Saturday 22 August, a Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by police travelled the wrong way along the A66 and collided head-on with a police vehicle.PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, were killed. So were all five people in the Passat: Michael Cahill, 23, Jakub Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae and Cole Worthy, both 17.Four of the five young men killed had amassed 30 convictions between them for offences including car theft, drug possession, assaulting police officers and driving offences. Cahill had no convictions.The chain of events that ended on the A66 is believed to have begun eight miles away, in a quiet suburban street in Acklam.It feels a world away from Grangetown. Hanging baskets and neat front gardens line the bay windows of 1930s semi-detached homes.Many residents are reluctant to speak. Why? Because of what happened to one house here that stands behind large metal barriers.A car was rammed into the bay window, exposing the room inside. Some of the other windows were also smashed.Fragments of lights and bumper remain scattered across the driveway.The home belongs to Cole Worthy's father, Gye Worthy, and the ramming happened on the same night Cole died.Police say the car used in the attack was a Volvo XC60. The BBC understands that Cole Worthy and the four others then set off in the Passat to find the Volvo.Now neighbours describe a street living in fear and say the home has been targeted for more than a year.There is no suggestion that Gye Worthy is involved in criminal activity.All but one of the residents who speak to us do so on the condition of anonymity. They are worried that showing their faces could place them or their homes at risk.What message do the attacks send to people on this street, I ask one."Well, they should be scared, shouldn't they, that something's going to happen to their property if they say anything or get involved. So we don't."Victoria, who moved here several years ago, says the escalating violence cannot be separated from the wider condition of the town."This is a social problem, especially in this area. Teesside has been massively neglected and ignored," she says.The attack in Acklam is far from Middlesbrough's only recent case of a vehicle being used as a weapon. Back in May, a tractor was driven into a house on Priory Road, and since the A66 crash Cleveland Police has investigated at least two further rammings.Detectives have also linked their wider investigation to a caravan fire on Attlee Road in Grangetown."It's getting worse," a nearby resident says. "They're always balaclava-ed up as well, do you know what I mean?"He blames drugs."It can't be anything else. Why would you be like you are unless it was drugs?" he says.Whether every incident is part of a single feud has not been established. But taken together, the rammings, fires and arrests have created a powerful sense that violence is being used to intimidate, punish and send messages.What is most unsettling for these residents is the sense that nobody is fully in control.Grangetown and South Bank are communities still living with the void left by the decline of heavy industry. Both now rank among England's most deprived neighbourhoods.In South Bank, we see a group of teenagers tend three ponies tethered on the grass. Two perform wheelies on electric scooters while another uses a long stick to scatter rubbish.On the adjoining estate, more than a dozen homes have boarded-up windows.On a wall are the words "RIP 2UZZI", said locally to have been the nickname of Jakub Matusiak, who lived one street away.One 17-year-old boy tells us he knew him. "He was my best mate," he says. "It's sad."Elsewhere, three letters are repeated: "FTP" - an expletive directed at the police.I ask the teenager if he would call the police if another young person approached him carrying a knife."No," he says. Before adding: "I've never needed the police in my life. I'd rather die than ring the police."Again and again, the young people we speak to express a profound distrust of the police.Cleveland's Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said what we'd heard was "horrifying"."Yes, there are a small minority of people in the Grangetown area who blight those communities. But we will continue relentlessly to serve our communities."The scale of the challenge facing the force and the community it serves is not new.The area has some of the highest police-recorded crime rates in England and Wales.Its leaders have been warning for years that its resources did not match the demands placed upon it.But recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.Since the crash, more than 200 additional officers have been deployed in Middlesbrough and surrounding communities. Their immediate task is to suppress the violence and identify those directing it.There is also the question of restoring order and rebuilding trust and confidence.As darkness settles over Grangetown, the quad bike is still circling the field and one woman, who moved here not long ago, asks us to move our car from outside her home, frightened we will be targeted and her property will become collateral damage.But what worries her more is her children's future. "I'm terrified my son will end up like them, he's only 10, I don't want him to grow up like that," she says gesturing to the lads with balaclavas tearing up the grass on the quad bike.Additional reporting by Brijesh Patel.

schema.headline: A66 crash: Distrust and fear hang over Middlesbrough

title: Thieves steal 70,000 pints of Guinness in two lorries
description: Thieves have stolen more than 800 barrels of Guinness by driving off from a depot with two HGV trailers. About 70,000 pints worth of the stout, estima
body: Thieves have stolen more than 800 barrels of Guinness by driving off from a depot with two HGV trailers. About 70,000 pints worth of the stout, estimated to be worth £115,000, were taken from Whitehouse Industrial Estate on Aston Lane in Runcorn on Monday, Cheshire Police said.One wagon-load was taken at about 19:45 BST and a second one was stolen at about 21:30.  The stolen barrels - which each would hold about 88 pints - had been destined for pubs, the force added. Det Sgt McClatchy said: "It is famously said that 'Guinness is good for you', but that is only the case when it has been bought and paid for."

schema.headline: Thieves steal 70,000 pints of Guinness in two lorries

title: Why are European countries moving their gold out of North America?
description: When the central bank of the Netherlands confirmed this week that it had moved tonnes of the country's gold out of North America, it said the relocati
body: When the central bank of the Netherlands confirmed this week that it had moved tonnes of the country's gold out of North America, it said the relocation would make it "better prepared for severe crises".Some 86 tonnes from the combined total of about 313 tonnes held in the US and Canada were relocated to London "in view of increasing geopolitical unrest", it said,  so the shiny stuff could be "readily available for use in a crisis situation".Questions were bound to follow. Why were the Dutch doing this? Were they anticipating some major economic shock on the horizon?It seems not, but the move was clearly in response to the unstable and uncertain state the world finds itself in, with trade and military wars prompting countries to take precautions and hold their gold closer to home.Earlier this year, France announced it had removed its gold reserves from the US to home shores. Meanwhile, Germany's Bundesbank transferred more than 216 tonnes of the metal from storage locations abroad - 111 tonnes from New York and 105 tonnes from Paris - over a few years ending in 2016., externalIt is a strategy which has played out before in times of global instability. "Some European central banks moved part of their gold holdings to New York during the Cold War," said research analysts Lina Thomas and Daan Struyven of Goldman Sachs.Joseph Cavatoni, senior market strategist at the World Gold Council, told the BBC while wars and trade tensions were "playing into some of these decisions", it didn't "top the list" of motivating factors.Inflation, interest rates and just having gold in a place where it can be traded quickly also played a role."I don't get a sense that there's an impending doom," Cavatoni said, "but what I do think is people are being better educated around how to manage their reserve assets, growing their reserve assets, and actually thinking more effectively around how to make the most of those assets."De Nederlandsche Bank said the gold removed from the US and Canada between March and August this year was now being held in the vaults of the Bank of England."We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness," said the governor of the Dutch central bank, Olaf Sleijpen.London was seen as the best choice due its position in the world as a major trading centre. If you want to be able to buy or sell gold fast in a crisis, London is the place to be, which makes the Bank of England a popular storage spot.The Bank is one of the largest custodians of gold in the world. Underneath the 300-year-old institution in central London sit about 400,000 bars worth more than £200bn.According to industry surveys by the World Gold Council, the Bank of England remains the most popular vaulting location, but central banks are increasingly diversifying where they store the precious metal.Where to store your country's gold is "increasingly top of mind for reserve managers", according to Thomas and Struyven of Goldman Sachs.In the modern world, there are many ways to shift your treasure around. The Dutch sold about 59 tonnes in New York and then bought more stocks in London, meaning that amount didn't need to be hauled across the Atlantic. But more than 27 tonnes were "physically transferred" from the US and Canada to the Dutch town of Zeist. A similar quantity was also sent from Zeist to London.Companies that perform such services are tight-lipped on how operations are carried out, but it's fair to say the security measures and planning are extensive to avoid the risk of a real-life Italian Job.Cavatoni, of the World Gold Council, said one standard approach to move gold stocks was to sell the commodity in one place and buy it in another. "Let's say I want my gold in New York and I have it in London. I could sell it in London, buy it in New York, same day, same time, effectively book transfer without actually having to put it on any other logistical change."There are only a few select companies which handle gold shipments across borders, one of which is Brink's Global Services, who told the BBC it had seen "increased demand" from the likes of central banks in recent times."Heightened geopolitical and economic uncertainty, along with gold's growing role as a strategic reserve asset, appear to be contributing to this trend," said Nader Antar, Brink's executive vice president.The reason gold storage is such a topic in the minds of central banks is because they have been increasingly buying the stuff. But storing it at home comes at a cost, said Thomas and Struyven of Goldman Sachs."Domestic storage requires investment in physical security, audit infrastructure, and insurance; costs that can be disproportionate for smaller central banks," they said.Over the past four years, central banks have accumulated an annual average of 1,000 tonnes of gold, up significantly from the 500 tonnes average over the preceding decade, according to the World Gold Council. The trend stretches back to the global financial crisis. And that is only expected to go up in the next year.Gold has been having a moment in recent years. Its price has surged to hit a series of record highs, passing $5,000 an ounce in January.There are several reasons behind its value jumping, but a major factor has been the precious metal's position in the human psyche as a so-called safe haven asset, to invest during periods of financial and geopolitical turmoil caused through trade and military wars.Inflation and interest rates also influence gold's popularity. Due to the commodity's scarcity and the value placed on it across thousands of years, it is somewhat resistant against rising prices, and so is seen as a good investment. "Over the past half-century, gold prices have risen much faster than the Consumer Price Index (CPI) - the most closely watched measure of inflation," according to investment bank Charles Schwab.While the price of gold has fallen from the record high seen early this year, it still remains at a high level historically.According to researchers at Goldman, the price is forecast to rise to $4,900 (£3,624) per troy ounce by the end of 2026, $300 more than it was in August. The demand for gold from central banks is one key reason why prices are surging, according to Thomas and Struyven.

schema.headline: Why are European countries moving their gold out of North America?

title: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?
description: Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined. These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see co-ordinate
body: Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined. These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see co-ordinated vandalism. Yet here, four surveillance cameras were attacked and cut down in the middle of the night.The metal poles were severed, leaving the distinctive black oval cameras and accompanying solar panels lying on the ground. On some of the cameras was a red sign reading: "Notice. 24/7 video recording."These cameras are run by a company called Flock Safety and this sabotage, which happened in late July, is a signal of growing concern over the nationwide spread of sophisticated AI-powered surveillance systems. Similar vandalism incidents have occurred in Minnesota, California and Georgia.Proponents say they have made communities safer and have helped dramatically increase the rate at which crimes are solved. But recent examples of misuse have caused concern. Critics say the cameras, which take pictures of the rear of every car that drives past, are overly broad investigative tools that treat civilians like suspects.They see the little black poles popping up in their neighbourhoods as visible reminders of state power, at a time when public confidence in institutions is historically low and many are concerned about the accelerating pace of technological change and the influence of AI on people's lives.Listen: ‘Big Surveillance’, Flock and ICEFounded in 2017, Flock Safety has become one of the country's biggest makers of Automatic Licence Plate Readers (ALPRs). These AI-powered cameras take a picture of the rear of every car that drives past. Footage is retained for a specified amount of time.But little is known about the extent to which Flock is being used - the company does not publish exact data, but says it works with more than 7,000 communities nationwide and estimates that there are approximately 100,000 cameras deployed.Records obtained by the BBC provide a rare glimpse into the extensive network of cameras and surveillance tech being used in America's fourth largest city, Houston, including the use of controversial facial recognition software powered by artificial intelligence.Flock is not just selling cameras - it is selling access to a database that can include thousands of cameras from around the country. Older ALPRs did not have this vast network, which is a major selling point for law enforcement.For example, Houston's Metro Transit Authority owns 35 cameras. But documents show Metro has access to around 20,000 devices in the Flock network - including some as far as Albany County, New York.And as Flock expands, so too can the scope of investigations. Documents released to the BBC show how the network has grown year-on-year. In the Cypress-Fairbanks independent school district, a typical licence plate lookup in April 2024 searched around 270 networks of cameras.By April 2025, the typical search scope had almost doubled to around 500 networks. In April 2026, 20% of searches were conducted across more than 6,000 networks.Critics in Houston say this national network concerns them more than individual cameras. Christopher Rivera, from the Texas Civil Rights Project, worries that authorities could use "these databases to search our everyday routines, which ultimately scrapes out our routes to work, where our children go to school, and where we worship - and that's very problematic".There have been recent incidents of privacy breaches that have caught national attention. Last week, a police officer in Kentucky was charged after using the Flock system to track his ex-girlfriend - who filed a protection order - over 2,000 times.He was caught using Flock's newly mandatory, AI-powered audit tool that flags suspicious use.Others are concerned about Flock being a way for police to avoid warrants, which are usually required to search a person's property or tap their phone. In 2025, a detective in Johnson County, Texas, searched over 80,000 images to locate a woman suspected of having an abortion. He did not have a warrant.CCTV cameras, licence-plate readers and surveillance are not new. But the scale of Flock's network and the integration of AI in modern surveillance tech is a recent development and it's turned Flock into a household name. Americans who otherwise ignored the cameras in their cities have started to notice and tune into the capabilities of the technology around them.With AI, unlike older licence-plate readers, law enforcement can search surveillance footage with a string of words like "Caucasian man, blue shirt" - not just a licence-plate image.One thing Flock does not use is facial recognition. But that does not mean police departments are avoiding that tech. Critics say it violates human rights, is susceptible to misidentifying innocent people, and can be biased against minorities.The BBC has received documents revealing that Harris County Sheriff's Office, which covers Houston, uses other facial recognition technology, Clearview AI. The tool includes a database of more than 70 billion images, many of which were scraped from public internet sources including social media. The documents, including purchase orders and a license agreement, show that the county's Clearview AI contract currently runs through to March 2027.Several European countries have issued the company with data protection fines, including a £7.5m penalty from the UK's Information Commissioner.Harris County Sheriff's Office use of this facial recognition technology has not been reported before. It did not respond to requests for comment.Police say surveillance technology like this, including Flock cameras, is important for fighting crime."It's a very good tool," says Chief Ray Schultz of the Memorial Villages Police Department - a small jurisdiction within Houston. "It makes the community safer." Before purchasing a Flock ALPR, his department would recover an average of three stolen cars a year. Now, this figure is 45, Schultz says.Some crimes solved in recent years would have been "impossible" without Flock, he adds. Last month, Schultz used the tool to find an elderly woman with dementia who had driven 60 miles from Galveston to Houston and had gotten lost. "We were able to find her and reunite her with her family."Schultz says that it is important for agencies to have strong policies governing ALPR use and officers that misuse the system should be held accountable."But don't throw out a tool that is valuable, that can help recover a missing child."Jasmine Khadem Gonzalez, an immigrant rights organiser, is worried that law enforcement might "use [the Flock] database to tell ICE where somebody is".The federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency does not have a contract with Flock directly. However, there have been reports of police officers citing "immigration" or "ice" as a reason for searching for a licence plate.Jessie, an immigrant from Central America, noticed a Flock camera outside her house last month. She asked the BBC to not use her real name out of fear it could impact a pending case to extend her green card."It makes me feel as if I'm being stalked," she says.In response, she's changed her commute to work. "I try to take different routes every day so there's not a pattern."But whether individual law enforcement agencies share info with the federal government is unclear. Federal immigration enforcement cannot access Flock data directly, Flock's CEO says. But some police departments have standing agreements with federal immigration enforcement to work together.In Harris County, a proposed Flock contract amendment initially included the explicit authorisation to share camera data with federal law enforcement, but this provision was later removed after push-back from campaigners.Some jurisdictions have opted not to renew contracts with Flock as a result of these concerns, including large metropolitan areas like Los Angeles, Seattle and Austin.In total, more than 200 communities have cancelled or not renewed their contracts since 2021 - including 90 in August alone - according to advocacy group Secure Justice, external. Their reasons for cancelling may include cost and concerns about data privacy. Nationally, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have suggested that there ought to be guardrails and several candidates have made it a campaign issue for the upcoming midterms. Republican Congressman Keith Self has proposed legislation that would require federal agencies to get warrants before accessing Flock data.The company itself has also amended some of its policies, such as requiring mandatory audits and reducing the default period that data stays on a server from 30 days to seven, unless flagged as part of an investigation. But individual agencies can choose to retain data for much longer.Flock's founder and CEO Garrett Langley told the BBC that it was up to individual cities to decide how long to store data and what information to share with whom."I don't think a technology company should be making decisions like that," he says."As long as it's a lawful investigation, we are not going to tell cities what laws they should or should not enforce."Flock is a safety, not surveillance, company, Langley says. Yet three patents filed between 2020 and 2025 have the word "surveillance" in the title.He boasts that the tech helped solve "about a million crimes" and helped find more than 10,000 missing people. "The debate of how we build a society where safety and privacy coexist" is worth having, he says, but the ongoing vandalism is "disappointing".But there is nothing Flock or law enforcement could say to make Jessie feel at ease with this technology, she says. "I just don't trust that they're doing it to keep us safe."

schema.headline: Flock says its cameras make US safer - so why are they being sabotaged?

title: Watch: US man struck by lightning describes 'horrific' experience

body: A man struck by lightning as he was walking down the street in Staten Island, New York, has described the experience as "horrific".Thomas Fahmy said he had been walking to the dentist on 27 August when he saw "a bright white flash" and instantly fell to the ground."I've never felt these sensations ever in my life", he told CBS News, BBC News's US partner.Fahmy was sent to hospital with the help of a local resident who called 911, and did not sustain serious injuries.

title: Retatutride: How the hunger for a new weight loss drug is feeding an industry of fakes
description: Excitement around the creation of a new drug, especially one showing early promise in clinical trials, is often celebrated by those developing it.But
body: Excitement around the creation of a new drug, especially one showing early promise in clinical trials, is often celebrated by those developing it.But new weight-loss drug retatrutide has become a headache not only for Eli Lilly, the pharmaceutical company behind it, but for regulators in the UK and around the world.The jab has not yet been approved for human use by any regulatory body.But illicit, counterfeit dupes of retatrutide are currently flooding the black market.Experts have told the BBC this is one of the first times they have seen copycat versions of an experimental drug, still in the throes of being tested, become so widely available.Vials purporting to be "reta" as it's become known, are being sold in the UK in gyms, nail and beauty salons, hairdressers, on social media and even by flower sellers on the street."The world has gone mad," pharmacist and director of 24 HR Pharmacy, Sehar Shahid says. "People are effectively injecting an illegal drug and thinking it's safe."It's become so normalised people openly talk about their dealers, where's best to get it from and post all over social media."One quick flick through my socials and I can order a batch of a drug billed as retatrutide in minutes - although I would have no proof what it's actually made of, what its effects would be and where it's come from.Keen users are posting before and after "reta" pics on their TikTok feeds, describing how it has silenced food noise, helped them shed pounds and lose inches, with some saying it's completely transformed their lives.The problem? Despite positive results in its most recent clinical trials, real retatrutide is still being tested for its safety and efficacy. Only 50% of drugs in this Phase III stage of testing in the US are eventually approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), so there is no guarantee retatrutide will ever hit the market. The high rate of failure is primarily down to drugs not working as well in large, diverse human populations as they do in smaller early tests, or because they reveal unexpected safety hazards.And the current, fake versions available may not resemble what's being developed in the safe confines of the laboratory.Eli Lilly's website carries a strong warning "no one should take anything claiming to be retatrutide outside of a Lilly-sponsored clinical trial". "Illicit retatrutide products may contain unknown ingredients, harmful contaminants and impurities. These products may also have too much or too little active ingredient, or the wrong ingredient entirely".Despite this, it seems there are plenty of people willing to take that gamble."Young fit patients are coming into hospital with nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, in some cases kidney failure," says endocrinologist, Prof Donal O'Shea.He says some personal trainers are not only supplying their clients with the drug, they are also injecting them with it."The patients have no idea how much they have been taking, or even what they've been injected with."Tom Davies says he nearly ended up in hospital after accidentally overdosing on a fake version of retatrutide. He ordered it from a Chinese supplier after friends at his gym recommended it."It was horrendous," says the 20-year-old from Brighton. "My body felt so under pressure, I was so bloated, it was like someone had dropped a 20kg weight on my stomach."For 72 hours I had really bad diarrhoea and nausea. I thought, if this continues I'm going to end up in A&E."Tom later realised he had given himself eight times the recommended dose. Depending on what is ordered, copycat retatrutide can arrive needing to be mixed with sterile, bacteriostatic water which requires various calculations.Dr Nas Khattak, a research doctor based in Chester, has been screening patients for one of Eli Lilly's Phase III clinical trials. He says those sourcing fake versions are in effect behaving as lab rats without any medical oversight."If users who buy it online become their own doctor, they're taking a huge risk," he warns.He says trial participants need to meet strict criteria before they are given the green light to start taking the real drug or a placebo."We request their GP record, we make sure that they're emotionally well. They'll have suicide, self-harm, mental health assessments - and this is all done by doctors."Then we come back and have a look at the blood tests, have a look at everything, and then we think whether they're suitable or not."Tom decided to do more research into dosing and, despite the nasty side effects he'd previously experienced, decided to give his fake version of retatrutide another go. After nine months of taking it in cycles, he says his cravings for sugar and junk food have gone.Pharmacist Shahid warns that just because a fake version of reta works for one person, does not mean it will "work for the next".The obesity drugs currently on the market - the likes of semaglutide (marketed as Ozempic and Wegovy), and tirzepatide (marketed as Mounjaro) - target just one or two hormone receptors. But, if approved, retatrutide will become the first weight loss medication in the world to act on three, giving it the nickname the "triple G".The three hormones it mimics are: GLP-1 - this slows down stomach emptying, signals fullness to the brain to reduce appetite and helps control blood sugar levelsGIP - this enhances insulin secretion and improves insulin sensitivity, and works alongside GLP-1 to help the body process nutrients and reduces hungerGlucagon - this is the hormone that's novel to retatrutide. It increases resting energy expenditure so the body burns more calories, promotes liver fat breakdown and supports weight loss.Lisa King has been taking a fake version of retatrutide since July and at one stage, while she was also going to the gym and eating healthily, she was losing 3kg (6lb) a week.It's also, she believes, helping her manage some of the symptoms of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). GLP-1s help regulate blood sugar, and some studies suggest these weight-loss drugs can help with some of the problems caused by PMOS, which can bring about extreme tiredness, kidney problems and high blood pressure."I'm not sure if it's due to reta," Lisa says, "but my sugar cravings have gone down, my periods have regulated and I've got a lot more energy."But retatrutide is still in trials. Does this bother her?"No," she says, "not at all. There are many things that have not been approved."If I start to experience any negative side effects I'll just come straight off it."Other users taking counterfeit versions of retatrutide have reported a range of issues including brain fog, nausea, diarrhoea, a loss of libido and no longer being able to feel any happiness or joy.Doctors are becoming increasingly worried about the side effects they are seeing amongst users of these counterfeit weight-loss drugs.Dr Sahira Dar, a GP and chair of the British Islamic Medical Association, says healthcare professionals should ask about black market products "without judgement", so patients feel able to "disclose what they have taken".Eli Lilly has been developing retatrutide for nearly 10 years. It is now fighting to protect its product and curb the illegal sales which are taking place across the world.It's taking action against peptide companies, influencers, compound pharmacies which manufacture the fake medication, and wellness clinics. It has reported more than 14,000 websites, advertisements and social media posts it says are illegally marketing the medication.Eli Lilly says it "continues to work with law enforcement and regulatory authorities to combat black market drugs".A spokesperson told the BBC: "Any retatrutide available online is unapproved, unverified and simply not worth the risk."The UK's Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) has carried out raids and made several seizures of "products claiming to contain retatrutide" over the past year.It says there are a number of different routes these products enter the UK and it is working to "disrupt illegal importation and distribution".But the sales continue.Prof O'Shea says while we need to "shine a light on the dangers of such black market drugs", we should not "trash this family of medications"."GLP-1s are a major advance in managing obesity, a major advance in our insight into how the brain regulates cravings and appetite."That," he says, "is huge".For now, there is still a long way to go before retatrutide gets approval anywhere.Eli Lilly plans to submit its application for US FDA approval early next year. It can take up to a year to carry out a review, so retatrutide would not be legally available in the US until the end of 2027 at the earliest.In the UK, depending on the approval of the MHRA, it could be on the market by 2028.

schema.headline: Retatutride: How the hunger for a new weight loss drug is feeding an industry of fakes

title: Jay-Z: Stars join US rapper at long-awaited UK show
description: Jay-Z also took a moment to thank his fans who have been there from the beginning, telling them that "music saved my life". His reflective mood contin
body: Jay-Z also took a moment to thank his fans who have been there from the beginning, telling them that "music saved my life". His reflective mood continued as he performed Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem) and Where I'm From, which explores his upbringing in the Marcy housing projects in Brooklyn, New York.He cranked the energy back up for his 2011 hit No Church in the Wild, which was amplified by fiery pyrotechnics that radiated heat through the stadium.Originally a collaboration with controversial rapper Ye, also known as Kanye West, Jay-Z left his voice in for the chorus but cut his verses out. US DJ Khaled had a brief moment on stage while Jay-Z changed, but it was the appearance of London-born rapper Giggs which got the crowd erupting. He appeared overwhelmed at one stage, his hand clutching his face, as he took in the packed crowd while performing his track Talkin Da Hardest alongside Jay-Z. The surprise guests didn't stop there, as Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean from the 90s American hip-hop collective The Fugees reunited to perform their hit tracks Ready or Not, Killing Me Softly with His Song and Fu-Gee-La.It was a full-circle moment for both them and Jay-Z as he recalled supporting them on their European tour. The US rap superstar closed out the night with rousing renditions of Public Service Announcement (Interlude) and Numb/Encore, hailing it as a "legendary night" that he would "never forget". The crowd appeared to agree as thousands praised him by holding up his famous diamond hand gesture.Fans had travelled from across the UK and the world to see the rapper, including Prince Dean Sithole, who hailed Jay-Z as one of his role models."I think he's very impacting, especially for us black people because we don't get a lot of recognition," the 19-year-old from Leeds told BBC Newsbeat."Seeing him today shows that dreams are possible and you can be that person that you want to be."Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, broke through with his 1996 debut album, but it was his third record, Vol. 2: Hard Knock Life, in 1998 which landed him the top spot in the US charts for the first time and a best rap album Grammy.He went on to establish himself as one of the most influential figures in hip-hop, releasing 13 solo studio albums and several collaboration records, which have secured him 25 Grammy Awards.He was also the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017, as well as being inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.Over the years, he has also become one of the most prominent music moguls in the world, with his company Roc Nation representing a host of top talent and, in recent years, it has been behind the Super Bowl half-time show.In 2019, he was declared hip-hop's first billionaire by Forbes, having built an empire based on music, property, fashion and investments alongside his wife Beyoncé.The power couple have three children, daughter Blue Ivy, 14, and nine-year-old twins, Rumi and Sir.

schema.headline: Jay-Z: Stars join US rapper at long-awaited UK show
